description_full: Ferrari N.V., through its subsidiaries, engages in design, engineering, production, and sale of luxury performance sports cars worldwide. It offers sports, track, one-off, and road cars, as well as supercars. The company also provides spare parts and engines, as well as after sales, repair, maintenance, and restoration services for cars; and licenses its Ferrari brand to various producers and retailers of luxury and lifestyle goods. In addition, it operates Ferrari museums in Modena and Maranello; Il Cavallino restaurant in Maranello; and theme parks in Abu Dhabi and Spain. Further, the company provides direct or indirect finance and leasing services; range of financial and ancillary services; special financing arrangements; and operates franchised and owned Ferrari stores. The company was founded in 1947 and is headquartered in Maranello, Italy.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 5K people. Revenue per employee of $1.4M ranks in the top quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers, improving at 10%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $361K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 6× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: Ferrari N.V. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $72.9B market cap on $8.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +15% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 31% against a 9% cost of capital — a 22-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $2.1B in free cash flow — roughly 26 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.47× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 9.8×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.8%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 32% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 3.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 30% operating margin runs 22pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 3.58x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+6.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 5% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.97, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $146.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 28% in the 2020 crash and 37% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $240 (margin of safety -74%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 24%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $184 to $319 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 37.6 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 29.8 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 35.1 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 12% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 12 covering analysts target $461 on average, 11% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 31% clears the cost of capital of 9.4% by 22pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.16).
It converts 26% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.47x.
ROE of 41% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.5x net debt to EBITDA ($1.6B of cash against $3.2B of debt), with interest covered 9.8x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 14.6% over 3 years and 15.4% over 5 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 12% of profits supports about 3.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 30.8% a year over five years.
Analysts expect 10.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 32.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 46%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.8% (1.0% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 10 consecutive years, raising it 20.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 5,752 employees, each generates about $1.4M of revenue, 3.6x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 9.7% a year.
That works out to $361K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $8.9M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
